\chapter{Asking a Question — Three Ways, and Which One to Use}
\label{ch:fr-questions}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask a question in French three ways — by raising my voice, with est-ce que, and by inversion — choose between them by how formal the moment is, and ask where, when, how, how much and why.}

The one question word that agrees with its noun, closing a chapter that began with the question costing no new words at all.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[une question]{une question — the question you make with your voice alone}

\label{lesson:FR-C32-intonation}



\begin{quote}
You can say a great deal in French and cannot yet ask anything. This chapter fixes that, and the first way costs you no new words at all.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
French has three ways to ask a question. This is the first, the cheapest, and by far the commonest in speech — and it costs you \textbf{nothing new at all}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tu parles français.}  — You speak French. \textbf{Tu parles français ?}  — You speak French?
\end{quote}

\textbf{The words are identical. The order is identical.} The only difference is that the second one rises at the end, and in writing, a question mark.

That is a real question, correct and unremarkable, and it is what a French speaker uses with friends, family, in a shop, all day. Note the space before the question mark — French puts a thin space before \texttt{?}, \texttt{!}, \texttt{:} and \texttt{;}, which English does not.

\textbf{Why start here.} Textbooks usually open with the formal inversion, which is the rarest of the three and the hardest to build. You can ask about anything you can already say, right now, by lifting your voice. Everything after this lesson is about \emph{register} and \emph{precision}, not about being understood.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{une question}
  \item \emph{Ask:} the same question all three ways you know so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you turn a French statement into a question with no new words? (\textbf{Raise your voice} at the end.) Is that correct French, or a shortcut? (\textbf{Correct}, and the commonest form in speech.) And what does French put before a question mark? (A \textbf{space}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[est-ce que]{est-ce que — the phrase that announces a question before it starts}

\label{lesson:FR-C32-est-ce-que}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous piece before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The second way. Put \textbf{est-ce que} in front of a statement and it becomes a question:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Est-ce que tu parles français ?}
\end{quote}

Nothing else moves. The statement stays exactly as it was; the phrase sits in front of it like a flag.

It is worth taking apart, because it looks like three words and behaves like one. Literally it is \emph{est-ce que} = \textquotedblleft{}is it that…\textquotedblright{} — French built a question marker out of a tiny sentence, then wore it down until nobody hears the parts any more. A speaker says it as one word, roughly \emph{ESS-kuh}.

\textbf{When you would choose it.} It is more neutral than the voice-only question and less formal than the inversion coming next — the safe middle. In writing, where your voice cannot rise, it is the ordinary way to ask.

English has no equivalent and does not need one, because English inverts instead: \emph{do you speak…}. That English \textbf{do} is doing the same job — a meaningless word inserted to mark a question — so the device is familiar even though the word is not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{est-ce que}
  \item \emph{Ask:} the same question all three ways you know so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{est-ce que} do to a statement? (Turns it into a \textbf{question}, with nothing else moving.) What is it literally? (\emph{Is it that…}) And which English word does the same job? (\textbf{Do}, as in \emph{do you speak}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[où]{où — where}

\label{lesson:FR-C32-ou}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous piece before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{où} — where
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Où est la gare ?} — Where is the station? \textbf{Tu vas où ?} — Where are you going?
\end{quote}

Both are correct. The question word can open the sentence or sit at the end where the answer would go, and the second is what you will hear far more in speech.

\textbf{Now the accent, which is not decoration.} French has two words spelled \emph{o-u}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ou} — \emph{or}
  \item \textbf{où} — \emph{where}
\end{itemize}

The grave accent is the \textbf{only} difference in writing, and in speech there is no difference at all: both are \emph{oo}. This is the one place in French where an accent does nothing to the sound and everything to the meaning, which is why it is never optional.

You now hold the first question word, and with it a question you can actually use on the first day in a French city.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{où}
  \item \emph{Ask:} the same question all three ways you know so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{où} mean? (\textbf{Where}.) What is the same word without the accent? (\textbf{Or}.) And do they sound different? (\textbf{No} — the accent is meaning only.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quand]{quand — when}

\label{lesson:FR-C32-quand}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous piece before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{quand} — when
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Quand est-ce que tu arrives ?} — When do you arrive?
\end{quote}

The \textbf{d} is silent. \emph{Quand} is \emph{kahn}, nasal, with nothing on the end — until the next word begins with a vowel, and then it comes back \textbf{as a t}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Quand est-ce que…} — \emph{kahn-TESS-kuh}
\end{quote}

That is \textbf{liaison}, and it is one of the things that makes fast French hard to cut into words: the consonants at the ends of words are silent alone and audible in company. Nobody writes it down; every speaker does it.

Latin \textbf{quando} is the ancestor, and it is worth spending: Spanish \emph{cuándo}, Italian \emph{quando}, Portuguese \emph{quando} — and the \emph{qu-} on all of them is the same Latin question-word opening you see in English \textbf{query}, \textbf{question} and \textbf{quest}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{quand}
  \item \emph{Ask:} the same question all three ways you know so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{quand} mean? (\textbf{When}.) Is the \emph{d} pronounced? (\textbf{Not alone} — but it returns as a \emph{t} before a vowel.) What is that called? (\textbf{Liaison}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[comment]{comment — how}

\label{lesson:FR-C32-comment}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous piece before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{comment} — how
\end{quote}

You already say it. \textbf{Comment allez-vous ?} is \emph{how are you}, and you learned it before you knew it contained a question word.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Comment tu dis ça ?} — How do you say that? \textbf{Comment ?} — on its own: \emph{Sorry?} / \emph{Pardon?}
\end{quote}

That last one is worth having. Used alone it is how a French speaker asks you to repeat — politer than \emph{quoi ?}, which is the blunt \emph{what?}

The origin is Latin \textbf{quomodo}, \textquotedblleft{}in what manner\textquotedblright{}, and English took the same idea by a different road: \textbf{mode}, \textbf{modal} and \textbf{manner} are all from \emph{modus}, the \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} half of it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{comment}
  \item \emph{Ask:} the same question all three ways you know so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{comment} mean? (\textbf{How}.) Which phrase you already knew contains it? (\emph{Comment allez-vous} — how are you.) And what does \textbf{Comment ?} alone mean? (\textbf{Sorry? / Pardon?})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[combien]{combien — how much and how many}

\label{lesson:FR-C32-combien}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous piece before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{combien} — how much, how many
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{C'est combien ?} — How much is it? \textbf{Combien de personnes ?} — How many people?
\end{quote}

\textbf{English splits this and French does not.} \emph{Much} for things you measure, \emph{many} for things you count — French uses \textbf{combien} for both and lets the noun sort it out. One word fewer to choose between, and one of the rare places French is simpler than English.

Note \textbf{combien de} before a noun. The \emph{de} is not optional and does not change for number: \emph{combien de personnes}, \emph{combien d'argent}.

\textbf{C'est combien ?} is the single most useful question in this chapter for a traveller, and it is three words long.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{combien}
  \item \emph{Ask:} the same question all three ways you know so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{combien} cover that English splits in two? (\textbf{How much} and \textbf{how many}.) What must follow it before a noun? (\textbf{de}.) And how do you ask a price? (\emph{C'est combien ?})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pourquoi]{pourquoi — why}

\label{lesson:FR-C32-pourquoi}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous piece before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{pourquoi} — why
\end{quote}

Take it apart: \textbf{pour} (\textquotedblleft{}for\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{quoi} (\textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}). \emph{For what?} French built its \emph{why} out of two words you can already see, and English does the same thing in \emph{what for?}

And the answer is built to match:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Pourquoi ?} — Why? \textbf{Parce que…} — Because…
\end{quote}

\textbf{Par ce que} is \textquotedblleft{}by that which\textquotedblright{}. So the question is \emph{for what} and the answer is \emph{by that which} — a matched pair, and the reason this book teaches them together rather than one now and one later.

That gives you the last of the five question words, and with \emph{parce que} you can now join two clauses into one sentence, which is more than a question: it is the beginning of connected speech.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pourquoi}
  \item \emph{Ask:} the same question all three ways you know so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{pourquoi} made of? (\emph{\textbf{pour}} + \emph{\textbf{quoi}} — \emph{for what}.) What answers it? (\emph{\textbf{Parce que…}} — because.) And what is \emph{parce que} literally? (\emph{By that which}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[parlez-vous]{parlez-vous — the third way to ask}

\label{lesson:FR-C32-inversion}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous piece before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The third and last way. Swap the verb and the subject, and join them with a hyphen:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tu parles français.} $\to$ \textbf{Parles-tu français ?} \textbf{Vous parlez français.} $\to$ \textbf{Parlez-vous français ?}
\end{quote}

This is \textbf{inversion}, and it is the form English used to have — \emph{speak you French?} — and lost, keeping it only in \emph{are you}, \emph{have you}, \emph{can you}.

\textbf{Where the three ways differ is register, not meaning:}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Tu parles français ?} — friends, family, shops. Commonest by far.
  \item \textbf{Est-ce que tu parles français ?} — neutral, and the default in writing.
  \item \textbf{Parlez-vous français ?} — formal, written, or deliberately polite.
\end{itemize}

A beginner is often taught inversion first and then sounds like a textbook in every conversation. It is the one you need to \textbf{recognise} immediately and can afford to \textbf{produce} last.

One sound rule: if the verb ends in a vowel and the subject begins with one, French inserts a \textbf{-t-} to keep them apart — \emph{parle-t-il}, \emph{a-t-elle}. It exists purely so two vowels do not collide.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{parlez-vous}
  \item \emph{Ask:} the same question all three ways you know so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three ways to ask a question? (\textbf{Voice}, \textbf{est-ce que}, \textbf{inversion}.) Which is commonest in speech? (\textbf{Voice}.) Which should you learn to recognise first and produce last? (\textbf{Inversion}.) And why the \emph{-t-} in \emph{parle-t-il}? (To keep \textbf{two vowels apart}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quel, quelle]{quel, quelle — which}

\label{lesson:FR-C32-quel}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous piece before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{quel} — which, what
\end{quote}

Every question word so far has been invariable. This one is not: \textbf{quel is an adjective}, and like every French adjective it agrees with the noun it asks about.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Quel jour ?} — Which day? \emph{(masculine)} \textbf{Quelle heure ?} — What time? \emph{(feminine)} \textbf{Quels livres ?} — Which books? \emph{(masculine plural)} \textbf{Quelles questions ?} — Which questions? \emph{(feminine plural)}
\end{quote}

\textbf{All four sound identical.} \emph{Kell}, every time. The agreement is entirely written — which makes it a spelling problem rather than a speaking one, and it is one of the commonest places a French exam takes marks off.

You already use one of these without thinking: \textbf{Quelle heure est-il ?} — what time is it. \emph{Heure} is feminine, so \emph{quelle} takes two \emph{l}s and an \emph{e}.

That is the fifth and last way this chapter teaches you to ask. Three structures, five question words, and one adjective that agrees.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{quel, quelle}
  \item \emph{Ask:} the same question all three ways you know so far
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \textbf{quel} change and \emph{où} does not? (\textbf{Quel is an adjective} and agrees with its noun.) Do the four forms sound different? (\textbf{No} — all \emph{kell}.) So what kind of problem is it? (A \textbf{spelling} one.)
\end{tcolorbox}
